मकवानपुरको भीमफेदी र बकैया गाउँपालिकामा निर्माणाधीन महादेवटार सुरुङको ब्रेक थ्रु समारोहलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै मन्त्री लम्सालले सरकारले द्रुतमार्ग निर्माणको काम तीन वर्षभन्दा बढी लम्बिएको हेर्न नचाहेको बताएका हुन्।

निर्माण व्यवसायीहरूलाई पटक–पटक अवसर र सुविधा उपलब्ध गराउँदा पनि अपेक्षित प्रगति हुन नसकेको भन्दै उनले अब काममा ढिलाइ गर्ने कम्पनीलाई छुट नदिने बताए। आयोजना निर्धारित कार्यतालिकाअनुसार अघि बढ्न नसक्ने अवस्था देखिए सम्बन्धित कम्पनीसँगको ठेक्का तत्काल तोड्न उनले निर्देशन दिएका छन्।

The government's planned decision on the construction model by mid-December is expected to be a key step toward determining how the long-awaited airport project will proceed.

चीनको दक्षिणी सहर शेन्जेनमा आयोजना हुने उक्त बैठक एसिया–प्रशान्त आर्थिक सहयोग (एपेक) शिखर सम्मेलनको अवसरमा हुन लागेको हो। यसअघि ह्वाइट हाउस र क्रेमलिनले समेत तीन नेताबीचको भेटवार्ताको तयारीबारे पुष्टि गरेका थिए। यद्यपि, चिनियाँ पक्षले बैठकको विस्तृत कार्यसूची र छलफलका विषय सार्वजनिक गरिसकेको छैन।

आणविक हतियारदेखि इरान युद्धसम्म छलफल हुने अपेक्षा
तीन नेताबीचको भेटवार्तामा आणविक हतियार नियन्त्रण, निशस्त्रीकरण तथा विश्वव्यापी भूराजनीतिक तनावका विषय प्रमुख रूपमा उठ्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

अमेरिकी राष्ट्रपति ट्रम्पले आणविक हतियारको भण्डार घटाउने विषयमा छलफल गर्न चाहेको बताइएको छ। साथै, उनले इरानमा जारी अमेरिकी युद्धको विषयसमेत बैठकमा उठाउने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

तर, रुस–युक्रेन युद्ध भने यसपटकको बैठकको मुख्य एजेन्डा नहुने सम्भावना रहेको जनाइएको छ।
युक्रेनबारे युरोपलाई पनि सहभागी गराउनुपर्ने जर्मनीको धारणा

युक्रेन युद्धसँग प्रत्यक्ष रूपमा प्रभावित युरोपेली मुलुकहरूलाई पनि सम्भावित वार्तामा सहभागी गराउनुपर्ने युरोपको धारणा रहेको यसले संकेत गर्छ।

चीनले त्यसपछि मात्रै आफ्नो आणविक हतियारसम्बन्धी वार्तामा सहभागी हुने संकेत दिँदै आएको छ।

अमेरिका, चीन र रुस विश्व राजनीतिमा प्रभावशाली भूमिका भएका तीन शक्ति हुन्। यी मुलुकका राष्ट्रप्रमुख एउटै टेबलमा बसेर छलफल गर्नु अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कूटनीतिका दृष्टिले महत्त्वपूर्ण मानिएको छ।

आणविक हतियार नियन्त्रण, इरान युद्ध र विश्वव्यापी सुरक्षा चुनौतीजस्ता विषयमा तीन नेताबीच कस्तो समझदारी बन्छ भन्ने चासो बढेको छ।

यद्यपि, बैठकबाट कुनै ठोस सहमति वा सम्झौता हुनेबारे अहिले नै निश्चित भइसकेको छैन। तीन शक्तिराष्ट्रबीचको यो भेटवार्ताले आगामी दिनमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सम्बन्ध र कूटनीतिक संवादको दिशालाई कसरी प्रभावित गर्छ भन्ने विषय महत्त्वपूर्ण रहनेछ।

The final number is 43. That is how many pilot whales died, according to the Department of Conservation. When rescuers reached the coast, four whales were still alive. Later, Project Jonah's Louisa Hawkes said all four had died, including the two that had been returned to the water.

CNN described it as a distressing mass stranding, and New Zealand has had many. The country is one of the world's strandings hotspots, and the cause of mass strandings is rarely known. Pilot whales are intensely social, and when one animal gets into trouble, the rest often follow. This is a correction for anyone who shared the early numbers: the toll was 43, not "dozens." Anyone who intentionally or negligently violates the law can face misdemeanor charges and a fine of up to $100,000.

The law does not immediately release captive orcas, but it prevents future breeding and establishes important restrictions on their captivity.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

 The 70-Foot Shot

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

It will hit televisions, radios, cable, and satellite systems across the country.
It will not go to cell phones.

The test is required by law at least once every three years.
This one was announced back on September 16.

The message will basically say: “This is a test… no action is required.”

Most people will hear the familiar tone, see the scroll, and move on.

But the timing is making some people raise an eyebrow.
Coming right after a major nationwide ground stop and in the middle of everything else going on… a few folks are asking why now.

Is it just routine maintenance of a critical system?
Or does the schedule feel a little convenient (or inconvenient) depending on how you look at it?

Either way, it’s happening today at 2:20 PM ET.

Anyone else find the timing odd?

Glenn, a member of the CIA’s Team Bravo, at Qala-i-Jangi in Balkh Province, Afghanistan, on November 25, 2001. Team Bravo had inserted into northern Afghanistan earlier that month, when Bob, Greg, and Glenn arrived at Sarob alongside Green Berets from ODA 534 to fight with General Atta’s forces.

On November 25, hundreds of al-Qaeda and Taliban prisoners held in the 19th-century fortress at Qala-i-Jangi, the “Fort of War,” rose up against their captors. Dostum’s men had never searched them properly. CIA officers Mike Spann and David Tyson were inside the fort questioning prisoners when the uprising began. Spann was overrun and killed, becoming the first American to die in combat in Afghanistan. Tyson fought his way out.

What followed was a six-day battle. The Americans and their partners called in airstrikes, AC-130 gunships pounded the fortress, and a misdirected JDAM wounded several of the men trying to retake it. It wasn’t until December 1 that the final 86 prisoners emerged from the cellar of the Pink House. Spann’s body was recovered on November 28.

The men who fought at Qala-i-Jangi were among the very first Americans on the ground after 9/11. Their story has been told, but never enough.

B-1 bomber pilots are now training in this little business jet…
and it’s giving them 100 extra flight hours a year. 

The B-1 Lancer is one of the most expensive aircraft in the Air Force inventory to fly.
Every hour in that bomber costs serious money — and those hours are limited.

So the Air Force came up with a workaround.

Near Dyess Air Force Base, B-1 pilots are now flying contractor-owned light jets (HondaJets) under a new program called BSTAR.
These smaller, much cheaper aircraft let them practice core flying skills — instrument work, handling, crew coordination — without burning through precious B-1 flight hours.

The result?
About 100 additional hours in the air each year for each participating pilot.

The expensive bomber hours stay focused on the things only a B-1 can do: aerial refueling, weapons employment, and combat tactics.

Some will say it’s a smart, cost-effective way to keep pilots sharp.
Others might wonder if training in a tiny business jet really prepares you for a 150-foot-long bomber.

Either way, the Air Force is betting that more time in the air — even in a smaller plane — is better than sitting on the ground.

Smart move?

A U.S. Army Green Beret from the 19th Special Forces Group in Afghanistan in 2002. If the beard looks familiar, you're not imagining it. This photo is widely said to be the inspiration for "Dusty," the bearded Tier 1 operator who became the face of the 2010 Medal of Honor game, cover art and all.

The 19th Group, one of the Army National Guard's two Special Forces Groups, sent its Green Berets to Afghanistan early in the war alongside their active duty counterparts. The men in photos like this did the real work long before anyone turned it into a video game.
Another operator from DEVGRU, the Navy's Special Mission Unit, from the same 2002 deployment guarding Afghan President Hamid Karzai, this time posing with a local Afghan.

Pontiac, Michigan. Inside the abandoned Pontiac Silverdome.

Before the historic 80,000-seat mega-stadium was imploded, operators from the Naval Special Warfare Development Group (DEVGRU / SEAL Team Six) were given the keys to the entire complex to run unrestricted live-fire counter-terrorism training.

Why an empty NFL stadium?

Because an 80,000-seat concrete dome introduces complex ballistic variables you cannot replicate on a flat shooting range:

Extreme Vertical Angles: Taking steep high-angle sniper shots from the 300-level upper deck down to targets placed on the 50-yard line.

Echoing Acoustics & Concrete Corridors: Navigating disorienting gunshot echoes, cavernous wind drafts, and blind concourse choke points.

Low-Profile Civilian Attire: Notice the operators are wearing blue jeans, flannel shirts, running shoes, and ball caps (including the operator in the foreground rocking a Detroit Lions hat)—matching the blended civilian profile used for domestic counter-terror response.

In the foreground, an operator sits with an Accuracy International precision bolt-action rifle mounted to the railing, while his spotter ranges targets through high-powered glass. Behind him, another team member works barricade transitions with a suppressed weapon platform.

No sterile shoot houses. No computer simulations. Just real-world concrete, steel, and elevation pushed to the absolute limit.

DEVGRU. Always evolving.

Fair winds and following seas to Freeman Johnson — the oldest surviving Pearl Harbor veteran, who passed away Saturday at age 106 in Centerville, Massachusetts.

On December 7, 1941, Johnson was a young Navy fireman working below deck on a boiler aboard the light cruiser USS St. Louis as the Japanese attack unfolded. His ship evaded midget submarines and fought its way out to open sea, and Johnson went on to witness Japan's surrender in Tokyo Bay from the USS Iowa in 1945.

Asked about his service years later, he stayed humble — saying, "I wasn't brave, I was there. I just did what I was told. I did my job." After the Navy, he married his wife Ruth, raised three daughters, served as a foster parent, worked 40 years in a machine shop, and didn't retire until 90.

Drop a salute in the comments for Freeman Johnson and the Greatest Generation.

Trump is heading to China this week for his third meeting with Xi Jinping in 2026.
Deal or no deal? 

First they met in Beijing in May.
Then in Washington in September.
Now it’s Shenzhen for the APEC summit on November 18-19.

Three face-to-faces in one year between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.

Trade. Tariffs. Technology. Rare earths. AI. Influence in the Pacific.
The list of unfinished business is long.

Some people think these meetings are just photo ops.
Others believe this is where the real leverage gets tested — who blinks, who walks away with something concrete, and who just kicks the can further down the road.

After everything that’s happened this year, a third meeting feels less like routine diplomacy and more like a high-stakes checkpoint.

The question isn’t whether they’ll smile for the cameras.
It’s whether anything actually moves.

Deal or no deal?

During high-stakes negotiations in Abu Dhabi mediated by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Washington is urging Moscow to allow European allies a formal seat at the table for upcoming rounds.

While Russia previously pushed to keep talks limited strictly to Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv, American officials insist that lasting security guarantees and regional stability require European leaders in the room.

Can an enduring peace agreement work without Europe at the table? Share your take in the comments below.

CNN is reporting, citing seven U.S. officials, that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C. — possibly using a "dirty bomb" or a chemical weapon.

Sources stressed the planning appears aimed at giving Tehran options rather than signaling an imminent attack, and officials are still debating whether Iran has the capability or intent to execute it. Still, two sources said the intelligence includes specific targets and locations, prompting contingency meetings over the past week as the Secret Service moved Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials into military housing.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," while Iran's U.N. Mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations as "false and fabricated."

How seriously should Washington treat this intelligence while Strait of Hormuz talks remain deadlocked?

America’s newest fighter jets just landed in Okinawa…
and they’re replacing more planes than they’re bringing. 

Two brand-new F-15EX Eagle IIs touched down at Kadena Air Base on November 15.
They’re the first of their kind permanently stationed overseas.

The plan is to bring in 36 of these advanced jets to replace the 48 older F-15s that used to call Okinawa home.

Newer technology.
Better sensors.
More weapons capacity.
Stronger electronic warfare systems.

On paper, it’s a clear upgrade.

But the numbers tell a different story too — fewer jets covering the same high-stakes region of the Pacific.

Some see a smarter, more capable force.
Others look at the math and wonder if “better” is enough when you’re still short a dozen aircraft in one of the most contested areas on the planet.

Kadena just got its first look at the future of American airpower in the Pacific.

Big upgrade… or too few jets?

A single line tucked into the U.S. Senate's proposed 2027 budget just revealed $77.1 million for a new nuclear bomb called the B94 — the first new American nuclear bomb designation since 1991.

Under U.S. naming rules, a "B" designation means an air-dropped bomb rather than a missile warhead or a minor upgrade to an existing weapon like the B61-13. Yet the 179-page appropriations document offers zero explanation of what the B94 is designed to do.

Defense analysts say it could be aimed at deeply buried, hardened underground bunkers — a capability gap the U.S. has wrestled with since canceling the Robust Nuclear Earth Penetrator in 2005 — though the Pentagon and NNSA have not confirmed its purpose.

Should the U.S. be developing new nuclear bunker-busters, or sticking to modernizing existing warheads?

An operator from DEVGRU, the Navy's Special Mission Unit, on Afghan President Hamid Karzai's protective detail in Kandahar on September 5, 2002. Wounded in the attack, he wrapped his own T-shirt around his head to stop the bleeding and stayed on the job.

Karzai was in his hometown that day for his younger brother's wedding. As his car pulled away from the governor's mansion, a gunman wearing an Afghan army uniform, one of the security guards around him, opened fire on the vehicle. Karzai's American bodyguards returned fire and killed the shooter within seconds. Karzai walked away unhurt. Kandahar Governor Gul Agha Sherzai and one of the American bodyguards were wounded, and one of Karzai's Afghan guards was killed in the exchange.

It was the second strike of the day. Only hours earlier, a car bomb had torn through a crowded Kabul shopping street, killing dozens. American special operators had taken over Karzai's protection only two months before, after Afghanistan's vice president was assassinated in Kabul. On September 5, that decision may well have saved the president's life.

While the FAA grounded every flight in America for over 4 hours…
Stephen King had a different explanation. 

On November 13, a nationwide ground stop hit the entire U.S. air system.
Thousands of flights delayed or canceled. Airports frozen. Travelers stuck.

The official reason? A telecommunications outage.

Stephen King wasn’t buying the boring answer.

He posted:
“The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic. They are blind but can hear like a motherfucker.”

Only Stephen King could turn a massive aviation meltdown into a horror-story one-liner that millions immediately shared.

Was it just a joke from the master of the creepy?
Or the kind of dark humor that hits a little too close when the whole country suddenly stops flying on a Friday the 13th?

Either way… the man knows how to grab attention.

Do you believe this?

The U.S. Army acknowledged in an urgent contracting notice Friday that American soldiers in the Middle East are "currently at risk" using non-standard personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers.
Now, the Army is moving on an expedited timeline to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers across five installation sites — one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon - within 45 days of a task order.
Each bunker will feature three sections of reinforced concrete, steel entrance doors, concrete Alaska barriers, and sandbagged exterior walls and roofs with at least 18 inches of overhead cover.
Why weren't hardened concrete bunkers already in place before troops were put in shipping container shelters?

VP Vance looked out over the border from a helicopter and said something simple:
“You just needed a new president.” 

No long speech.
No complicated new legislation.
Just a clear statement.

According to Vance, securing the border wasn’t some impossible puzzle that required years of new laws.
It took political will.

He pointed to the lowest border crossings in recent history and the removal of thousands of criminal illegal immigrants as proof that the difference came down to who was in charge.

Some people will hear that and nod.
Others will push back hard and say it’s never that simple.

But the line itself is hard to ignore:
After years of debate, hearings, and failed bills… one side claims the real missing piece was leadership.

Whether you agree or not, it’s a direct challenge to the idea that the border problem was too complex to solve.

Agree?

An assaulter from Joint Task Force 2 stands beside a commercial airliner used to rehearse aircraft takedowns and other scenarios during training. JTF 2 is Canada's Special Mission Unit, and hijacked aircraft are exactly the kind of crisis it exists to resolve.

On October 3, 1993, Chief Warrant Officer Mike Durant was flying Super 64 — an MH-60 Black Hawk with the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment — when an RPG hit the tail rotor over Mogadishu.

The crash killed crewmates Bill Cleveland, Ray Frank, and Tommy Field. Badly injured with a broken back and a compound femur fracture, Durant was defended on the ground by Delta Force snipers Gary Gordon and Randy Shughart, who gave their lives holding the site and were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.

Held captive for 11 days, Durant was the only American taken alive that day. He returned to flying, retired in 2001 as a CW4 Master Aviator after 22 years of service including Just Cause and Desert Storm, wrote In the Company of Heroes, built Pinnacle Solutions in Huntsville, and later ran in Alabama's 2022 Republican U.S. Senate primary.

33 years later, his story remains a tribute to the Night Stalkers and Delta operators who never made it home. Night Stalkers Don't Quit.

Leaving the White House for his Asia trip on Monday, President Donald Trump told reporters he "may" bring up the espionage allegations surrounding former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

At the same time, Trump noted that the claims remain unproven — saying, "I don't know that she is a spy. ... Nobody's proven that" — and added he would not mind seeing former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12 amid reports of his relationship with Alice Huang and U.S. intelligence scrutiny over whether Megaspeed was linked to restricted AI chip transfers. Both Beijing and Megaspeed have denied the allegations, and the Justice Department has not reached a conclusion.

Should Trump raise the Megaspeed and Nvidia investigation directly with Xi Jinping, or keep it separate from trade talks?

Back in June 2012, a Texas father rushed to his 5-year-old daughter's screams on a ranch near Shiner — and caught a 47-year-old acquaintance sexually assaulting her.

The father pulled the man off his child and fatally beat him with his bare hands before calling 911. Lavaca County Sheriff Micah Harmon and District Attorney Heather McMinn confirmed that physical evidence and witness accounts backed up the father's account, and a Lavaca County grand jury declined to bring any charges.

Under Texas law, deadly force is justified when reasonably necessary to stop an ongoing sexual assault or aggravated sexual assault.

Do you agree with the grand jury's decision not to indict?

One day a Tomb Guard told Defense Secretary Hegseth’s group to be silent.
The next day, Hegseth pinned a medal on him. 

On Veterans Day at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias was doing what Tomb Guards do every single day — protecting the silence and the respect that place demands.

When members of Hegseth’s group were talking and laughing nearby, Iglesias called out clearly:
“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

No drama. No hesitation. Just the standard.

The very next day, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth invited members of The Old Guard to the Pentagon and awarded Spc. Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal.

His message was simple:
“We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist.”

In a time when a lot of people seem confused about what’s sacred and what’s not, this moment stood out.

A soldier did his job without fear or favor.
And the Secretary of Defense didn’t just accept it — he honored it.

Sometimes the quietest standards speak the loudest.

The U.S. Army is taking a massive leap into maritime strike warfare—preparing to acquire up to 100 unmanned surface vessels and attack drones as it shifts its primary operational focus to the Indo-Pacific, according to reporting from The War Zone and Militarnyi.

While ocean warfare is traditionally Navy territory, the Army’s "hidden navy" and Army Special Operations are rapidly fielding autonomous maritime platforms. During recent combat exercises in the Philippines, Green Berets from the 1st Special Forces Group successfully operated one-way maritime attack drones to strike and sink target vessels near critical strategic chokepoints.

Led by the 8th Theater Sustainment Command and forward-deployed units in Japan, the military plans to pre-position autonomous transport vessels and lethal strike drones across key hubs—including Japan, the Philippines, South Korea, and Australia—to keep remote island detachments supplied and turn littoral waterways into lethal minefields for adversary warships.

Is the Army's push into maritime drone swarms the ultimate asymmetric equalizer in a Pacific conflict, or should littoral naval combat remain strictly under the Navy and Marines?

Is Everyone Overreacting to the 2026 Midterms?You’ve probably seen the posts calling this election a historic disaster for Republicans.
But take a look at the actual House numbers:Bill Clinton lost 54 seats in 1994  
Barack Obama lost 63 seats in 2010  
Donald Trump just lost 41 seats in 2026

Forty-one is a clear loss. No question.
But it’s not the biggest midterm seat drop in recent decades. Presidents almost always lose seats in the House during midterms. That’s been the pattern for a long time.So when people treat 41 seats like the end of the world, it feels a bit overblown if you’re only looking at the House.That said, the full picture is more complicated.
Democrats also flipped the Senate and won some surprising races in traditionally red states. Those results matter and give the other side real momentum.Still, the pure House seat count that everyone’s screaming about isn’t as unprecedented as the reactions suggest.

He started out working the fields on a Georgia farm—and went on to lead the U.S. Navy Blue Angels.

After his first application to the Blue Angels was turned down, Donnie L. Cochran reapplied a year later and was selected in 1985 as the team's first Black pilot. In November 1994, he made history again by returning as the squadron's first Black commanding officer and #1 flight leader.

From Pelham, Georgia to Jet #1—drop a salute in the comments for Capt. Donnie Cochran.

#BlueAngels #USNavy #DonnieCochran

Whitehall, London. Outside 10 Downing Street.

Two decorated alumni from The Shawn Ryan Show representing the very pinnacle of American and British Tier-1 Special Operations reunited in London:

On the Left: Former U.S. Army Delta Force (1st SFOD-D) operator Kyle Morgan—recipient of the Distinguished Service Cross for his heroic counter-assault during the 2015 Radisson Blu hotel terrorist siege in Bamako, Mali, and founder of Blu Bearing Solutions.

In the Center: A UK Metropolitan Police Authorised Firearms Officer (AFO) on armed counter-terror security duty outside the Prime Minister’s residence, carrying a SIG Sauer MCX platform.

On the Right: Former British 22 Special Air Service (22 SAS) operator Jay Cal (featured on SRS Episode #214)—veteran of both the Royal Marines and the SAS Regiment.

The bond between Delta Force and the 22 SAS is the closest brotherhood in modern military history.

In the late 1970s, Colonel Charles Beckwith served on exchange with the British 22 SAS in the jungles of Malaya. Inspired by their selection and counter-terror tactics, Beckwith returned to the U.S. and built Delta Force using the SAS model as its foundation.

From the streets of Baghdad during Task Force Black to covert joint target interdictions across the globe, Delta and the SAS have hunted together in the dark for decades.

"Who Dares Wins."

The three-star general in charge of Air Force training just made his No. 1 priority crystal clear — getting newly trained Airmen to be more like Marines.

Speaking at a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies event Monday, Air Education and Training Command boss Lt. Gen. Clark Quinn said he wants to build a stronger Airman identity by having new recruits emulate the culture of the Marine Corps — while also rolling out iPads and AI-assisted study tools for Gen-Z trainees.

Can you really build Marine Corps culture inside the Air Force, or are the two branches just wired differently?

He fled Vietnam as a 4-year-old refugee.
Now he wants to run the entire U.S. Navy. 

Hung Cao’s story is the kind America used to celebrate without hesitation.

His family escaped Vietnam when he was just four years old.
He grew up, joined the Navy, became a captain, and later entered politics.
Today he is the Acting Secretary of the Navy — and he’s asking the Senate to confirm him permanently.

On November 17 he sat through a tough confirmation hearing.
Senators from both parties pressed him hard on readiness, long deployments, the strain of ongoing operations, and whether he has the right vision for the fleet.

Some see a classic American success story: a refugee who rose through the ranks and now stands ready to lead the world’s most powerful navy.
Others have serious questions about his recent performance as acting secretary and whether he needs more distance from active-duty service.

The Senate will decide soon.

A refugee who arrived with almost nothing is now one step away from becoming Secretary of the Navy.

Should the Senate confirm him?

Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

“VIOLENT STORM OVERWHELMED VESSEL: AIR FORCE EOD JUMPMASTER SAVES DROWNING SURVIVORS AT SEA.”

When a violent ocean storm hit with mountainous swells, freezing temperatures, and treacherous rip currents, people were thrown into the open sea and within minutes of drowning. Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer dove straight in.

An elite Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) flight leader and the first EOD technician in U.S. Air Force history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Riemer was at sea when disaster struck:

Hearing desperate cries for help, Riemer immediately plunged into the freezing, turbulent ocean, battling massive swells and rip currents to reach the scattered victims.

Reaching the survivors, Riemer used water survival techniques to keep them afloat, quickly assessing that two airmen had exhausted their strength and were moments away from slipping beneath the surface.

Fighting Back with Flotation Gear: Riemer fought his way back through the punishing waves to the boat, retrieved emergency life preservers, swam back into the violent sea, and secured the drowning victims in flotation vests.

 Swimming against powerful currents, he towed the victims through the swells to within 25 meters of the vessel, secured a heavy safety line, and hauled them safely aboard before ensuring everyone was accounted for on the return to port.

In March 2025, Brigadier General Brian Hartless presented Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer with the Airman’s Medal—the Department of the Air Force's highest decoration for heroism outside of combat.

A combat veteran of Operations Enduring Freedom, Inherent Resolve, and Freedom's Sentinel, Riemer currently serves as the Senior Enlisted Leader for the Air Force Civil Engineer Center EOD Division at Tyndall Air Force Base, where he was also named the 2024 AFMC Outstanding EOD Master Blaster of the Year.

Trump just noticed the gas price drop… and questioned the timing.

Gas prices have fallen sharply.
According to AAA, the national average is now around $3.75 a gallon — down roughly 55 cents in the past month.

Trump’s response?
“Notice that they waited until after the ‘election?’”

He offered no evidence that the drop was deliberately delayed.
In reality, prices had already been trending downward in the weeks leading up to Election Day, driven by normal seasonal factors, higher production, and lower demand.

Still, the comment landed exactly as intended.
When prices are high, politicians get blamed.
When they fall, the same politicians often claim credit — or in this case, raise suspicions about the timing.

Whether you see it as a fair question or classic political deflection, one thing is clear:
Gas prices remain one of the most emotionally charged numbers in American politics.

What do you make of the timing claim?

What started as a late-night food run turned into a lifesaving rescue when three U.S. Marines stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort pulled an unconscious driver from a burning pickup truck on Parris Island Gateway.

The Beaufort County Sheriff's Office honored Cpl. Nathan C. Armstrong, Cpl. Isaac T. Ames, and Cpl. Caleb L. Crawford—alongside a responding sheriff's deputy—with Life Saving Awards and medals for their actions during the Aug. 3 fiery crash.

Semper Fi to these three Marines—drop a salute in the comments.

#USMC #Marines #SemperFi

Capt. Derek Herrera had vowed to leave the Marine Corps the same way he entered it: on his own feet. Aided by robotic leg braces, this Marine, paralyzed from the chest down by a sniper in Afghanistan, walked across a parade ground at Camp Pendleton to receive a Bronze Star for bravery. Herrera, 30, a Naval Academy graduate, is set to retire next week. He is studying for an MBA at UCLA and plans to become involved in helping veterans. "Your drive and determination are great, and you will continue to do great things," Lt. Col. John Lynch told Herrera. Some 300 Marines and other guests watched in respectful silence as Herrera, his wife Maura, and his service dog Shaggy arrived at the ceremony. The only sound was the soft whirring of the robotic system's motors. Herrera is the first person in the country to purchase a ReWalk system, according to the manufacturer, ReWalk Robotics Ltd.

The duct-taped American Airlines passenger just had his state charges dropped.

You remember the video.
A passenger completely wrapped in duct tape and zip ties, restrained in his seat after an alleged mid-flight meltdown.

On a September 3 American Airlines flight from Dallas to Newark, Arthur “Layne” Lundeen is accused of launching into racial slurs, anti-gay insults, and disruptive behavior toward the crew.
Fellow passengers eventually taped him down.
The flight was forced to divert to Baltimore.

Maryland had charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.
Those state charges have now been dropped.

Prosecutors say the incident happened in the air, so it falls under federal jurisdiction.
He still faces federal charges for interfering with the flight crew.

The viral video made the story famous.
The legal outcome is turning out more complicated than a lot of people expected.

What do you think about the charges being dropped at the state level?

FORT BENNING, Ga. (APRIL 24, 2013) -- The family of Sgt. 1st Class Kenneth Westbrook was presented with his Silver Star for gallantry, and his second Combat Infantryman Badge, April 19, during an emotional ceremony at Derby Auditorium here.

Westbrook died Oct. 7, 2009, as a result of wounds suffered Sept. 8, 2009, when insurgents attacked his unit in the Ganjgal Valley, Afghanistan.

With the award coming nearly three and a half years after his death, Westbrook's wife, Charlene, said she felt an immense sense of pride in her husband.

"I would say that I'm so very proud of him and that he's my hero," she said. "Actually, he'd probably grimace and say, 'No, I'm not a hero. I'm just doing my job.'"

The Silver Star is the Army's third highest award for gallantry, behind only the Distinguished Service Cross and the Medal of Honor.

“End of an era.”
The Navy is discontinuing the peacoat after more than a century. 

That heavy, double-breasted wool coat has been part of the Navy’s look for generations.
Starting October 1, 2027, it will no longer be authorized.

The same goes for the officer reefer coat.
Both are being replaced by a modern synthetic parka.

The change is part of a larger effort to lighten the seabag and simplify what sailors have to carry and maintain.
Navy message NAVADMIN 270/26 lays it out clearly.

For a lot of people who served, the peacoat wasn’t just a coat.
It was the thing you put on when the weather got nasty, the one that showed up in photos, the one that felt like the Navy.

Now it’s being phased out for something lighter, more practical, and easier to maintain.

Tradition versus efficiency.
Another small piece of the old Navy is moving into history.

How do you feel about losing the peacoat?

Sfc. Hester is one of the few women to be awarded for valor in close-quarters combat.

Leigh Ann Hester was a sergeant with the National Guard’s Kentucky-based 617th Military Police Company when she was deployed to Iraq, and in 2005, she was scanning and clearing a route for a supply convoy near Baghdad when her squad was ambushed by enemy fire.

She was trained for this, as it was a risk that came with her daily job in Iraq. Thus, when they became under attack, she knew exactly what to do. She directed her team away from the enemy’s intense fire and into a flanking position that exposed multiple irrigation ditches and an orchard that the enemies were using to stage the attack.

She was initially directing fire, then began fighting on foot. Sgt. Hester displayed incredible bravery as she had walked directly into the line of fire to kill at least three enemy combatants at close range, resulting in numerous convoy members lives saved. With thirty-three insurgents killed or wounded and one captured, every member of her unit survived.

Her heroic actions led her to become the first woman since World War II to earn the Silver Star Medal and the very first to ever earn it for combat valor.
Sgt. Hester separated from the National Guard and became a police officer after she returned to the United States; a job she had wanted since childhood. But she enjoyed being a soldier so much so, that she rejoined the National Guard shortly after.

In 2014, she spent 18 months in Afghanistan, where she was promoted to sergeant first class. And in 2017, she was sent to the Virgin Islands as part of the international humanitarian effort in the wake of Hurricane Maria.

“12,000 FEET UP A FROZEN MOUNTAIN: HE CARRIED HIS PARALYZED TEAMMATE DOWN TO AN IMPROVISED LZ.”

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

 The 70-Foot Shot
The Coordinated Ambush: On October 12, 2022, three officers from the Bristol Police Department responded to a staged 911 call on Redstone Hill Road. As they approached, a gunman concealed in the darkness ambushed them with a semi-automatic AR-15 rifle, firing over 80 rounds of high-velocity ammunition in seconds.

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Staging his handgun over the cruiser’s rear quarter panel, he acquired his sights in the darkness, tracked the gunman at roughly 70 feet (23 yards), and broke a single 9mm trigger press directly into the shooter’s head, ending the ambush instantly.

Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time. 

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq. 

When these IEDs exploded, three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles. 

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices. 

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow-on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance. 

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush. 

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist. 

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience. 

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

Warfle distinguished himself by exceptionally valorous achievement as a Ranger Squad Automatic Weapons Gunner on August 18, 2010 while deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. Specialist Warfle was assigned to a task force, whose mission was to capture or kill Al Qaeda (AQ) and Taliban (TB) Senior Leadership. Specialist Warfle's valorous actions under effective fire while executing an objective saved the lives of his teammates and were instrumental in the death of at least 16 Taliban fighters, the removal of two Taliban Provincial Commanders, and the recovery of a large cache of weapons intended for use against Coalition Forces. On August 18, 2010, the team received special intelligence indicating that a Taliban Commander and weapons facilitator, was meeting near a tree line with at least 17 other Taliban fighters. Information gathered indicated that the enemy was orchestrating an ambush on Coalition Forces in Logar Province, Afghanistan. The team observed the fighters in position for the attack to include multiple spotters and runners used to communicate between the various fighting locations. The Battle Space Owner was notified of the imminent threat and diverted all convoys. When the enemy fighters aborted their attack they were observed walking in a military formation back towards a meeting site along a tree line. En route to that location the enemy fighters were positively identified to be carrying weapons. The team initiated a kinetic strike on the fighter's location from two AH-64s. The team stood ready and boarded two CH-47 helicopters for insertion once the kinetic strike was complete. Immediately after the kinetic strike, the team inserted a Ranger Element onto the hot landing zone to the West of the target area to eliminate the several remaining enemy combatants. Ranger Element 1, consisting of Specialist Warfle and five others, were tasked with isolating the Northern side of the tree line and suppressing the enemy to allow Ranger Element 2 to assault from West to East. Upon infiltration the Ranger Assault Force received effective enemy fire in vicinity of the North-South running tree line where the AH-64s had just completed gun runs. As soon as Specialist Warfle stepped off the ramp he came under fire from multiple enemy positions and without hesitation returned fire and crawled 15 meters through the muddy field towards the enemy. From this position, Specialist Warfle suppressed the multiple enemy positions with 150 rounds from his MK-46 allowing Ranger Element 1 to move to the North and Ranger Element 2 to maneuver to the South. Under fire and with no cover in the open field, Specialist Warfle continued to suppress the enemy positions permitting members of the Assault Force to get down in the prone position while the leaders determined a way to assault the enemy positions. After a couple of minutes passed, Ranger Element 2 came under heavy effective fire from enemy crew served weapons. Realizing that Ranger Element 2 was effectively pinned down in the open field to the South, Specialist Warfle moved with Sergeant Lugo to the North to flank the enemy position from the North-West. Specialist Warfle, while under heavy effective enemy fire, advanced on the enemy position to suppress the enemy and allow the Assault Force to maneuver on and destroy the entrenched enemy. As Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle voluntarily maneuvered towards the enemy positions they identified two entrenched enemy personnel with automatic weapons firing on the Assault Force. Specialist Warfle continued to advance on the entrenched enemy using suppressive fire alone to protect Sergeant Lugo and himself because there was no available cover in open terrain. When Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle got within 25 meters of the enemy machine gun positions, Specialist Warfle and Sergeant Lugo were both hit with a volley of machine gun fire. Although Specialist Warfle knew he had been shot in the right shoulder he disregarded his own personal safety and moved through the kill zone to Sergeant Lugo's side to protect his incapacitated Squad Leader. Specialist Warfle purposefully positioned himself in the line of enemy fire and immediately suppressed the enemy in order to defend Sergeant Lugo and provide covering fire for the platoon medic, Sergeant Solomon, to move to and treat Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle fearlessly continued to provide accurate suppressive fire from his exposed position, allowing Staff Sergeant Myers and Sergeant Kochli the ability to move forward, suppress the enemy, and then subsequently evacuate Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle continued to provide suppressive fire as Sergeant Solomon, Staff Sergeant Tucker, and Sergeant Kochli pulled Sergeant Lugo back to cover. Specialist Warfle bounded back to the West over the open field while the Assault Force provided suppressive fire. Specialist Warfle's actions allowed the Assault Force to break contact, drop ordnance on the enemy positions, and safely move to the exfiltration hot landing zone. By repeatedly risking his life for others, Specialist Warfle's purposeful gallant actions, selfless dedication to the safety of his teammates, and demonstrated extraordinary heroism were distinctive and exemplary. Through his distinctive accomplishments, Specialist Warfle's personal actions reflect great credit upon himself, his unit, and the United States Army.

Surrounded and severely outnumbered in combat, you can either give up or fight to the death. Petty Officer Luttrell and three other SEALs faced that decision in the hills of Afghanistan on June 28, 2005. A SEAL never gives up!

The team, which included Lt. Michael Murphy and Petty Officers Matt Axelson and Danny Dietz, had been sent on a covert mission to find and kill a Taliban leader. As the SEALs scoured the area, they encountered three civilians who Luttrell believes alerted Taliban fighters. About an hour later, approximately 80-100 Taliban fighters appeared and began a ferocious assault. As the small team fought back, a Chinook helicopter arrived in support – but was shot down by the enemy, killing all 16 men on board.

The SEALs realized that their odds of survival were slim – but their training and sense of honor told them to take out as many enemies as they could. By the end of a two-hour gunfight that careened through the hills and over cliffs, Murphy, Axelson, and Dietz had fallen.

An estimated 35 Taliban were also dead. Luttrell managed to escape the carnage – badly injured – and slowly crawl away down the side of a cliff.

Dehydrated, with a bullet wound to one leg, shrapnel embedded in both legs, three vertebrae cracked; the situation for Luttrell was grim. Rescue helicopters were sent in, but he was too weak and injured to make contact. Traveling seven miles on foot, he eventually reached a village where he was put under “lokhay warkawal,” Afghan for the protection of the villagers, who fed him and cleaned his wounds. In short order, one of the villagers made his way to a Marine outpost with a note from Luttrell, and U.S. forces launched a massive rescue operation that pulled him from enemy territory. To this day, Luttrell remains indebted to the villagers who risked their lives in his defense. As he told The Washington Post, “In the middle of everything evil, in an evil place, you can find goodness. Goodness. I’d even call it godliness.”
